AMD doesn't just get beat up at SYSMark

True but a lot of that is down to the way AMD hardware differs in layout from Intels, AMD cores shares so much resources between pairs of integer cores that if you queue up instructions poorly (or I should say not carefully enough) you'll end up with one core hogging a lot of resources (usually the FPU or L2 and L3 caches) which causes a delay on the other core within the same module. Most of this was fixed with the post Steamroller variants doing much much better and instruction decoding and intellegently predicting what threads are best suited wehre but its just an inherent design quirk of all Bulldozer variants that has to worked with or else you're going to get really inefficient usage. Its why an early work around for less than spectacular performance (worse than Phenom II performance) was to disable every second core leaving one active per module, even Windows 7 had to be patched specifically for Bulldozer processors or it caused substantial performance problems.

A lot of games and benchmarking software should have been patched or at least build with it in mind and we are seeing it become the norm now but it took so long the damage has been done, the simple fact is even if AMD did continue making flagship desktop CPU's the same old benchmark games and software tools would shit all over AMD while showing Intel hardware with praise. Mark my words even if Zen is the fastest most efficient processor on the market Intel will still coax reviewers into using Intel approved software giving unfair comparisons in stupidly subjective comparions.

I think an important distinction you have to make is that Bulldozer and basically everything AMD's done since X2 has been trying to squeeze more performance out of less components. The interdependency you describe is because of architectural decisions AMD to be cheap, not powerful; rewriting the Windows scheduler and a bunch of benchmark programs to address this architecture in a specific way to bring it up to...well, still sub-Intel realms is the reason they're faltering now. It's not just numbers on synthetic benchmarks that are poor; AMDs fall short of comparable Intels in almost every real-world test they get put through, and the difference gets worse and worse as you move up the processor line.

I don't know what the answer is for AMD. It can't be 'git gud' because they don't have the fabs or the cash or the brainpower or the R&D budget to really go head to head with Intel, but at the same time from their quarterlies it doesn't seem like making chips for consoles and other embedded devices is all that lucrative. I really want a competitor for Intel and for NVidia both just to keep them honest both price-wise and innovation-wise.

Well if you're going to say that about AMD's products you've got to say the same is true for Intel, they've just taken two routes to similar results. Bulldozer is about sharing pieces of hardware between two or more physical processor cores where as Intel has taken a split one core into two approach to get more from the silicon without having a more expensive part, its not quite that simple but its essentially true. Interesting little fact Intels hyperthreading is a division of labor across the massive ALU, essentially giving it two jobs in one clock cycle allowing the single integer core to get more done, AMD overcame some of the Bulldozer limitations by doing something very similar with the FPU to allow two integer cores to use the FPU in one clock cycle and cut down on the waiting around.

to be cheap, not powerful

Well it is powerful and for its power quite its cheap so saving die space (which costs money) by having components shared was a sensible choice that yielded a pretty good processor, alright it did have more than a few big and small problems that needed addressing but AMD really couldn't afford to chase Intels tick tock cycle which is why we never got flagship desktop Steamroller and Excavator CPU's. Bulldozer was a server part released as mainstream hardware so it had some half baked ideas that worked well when you've got all your ducks in a row but not so well when you're fighting an uphill battle of entrenched development methods and a "pro-sumer" media being very selective in how it compares AMD products to Intel products.

There was going to be a Piledriver(28nm) and Excavator(28nm an alt process) AM3+ processors which were canceled so AMD's "best", even the best APU's don't have the same cache sizes the FX8xxx have. Its always going to look a bit less than fantastic vs Intels current gen hardware which isn't helped by shit benchmarks being used to make things look much much worse than it really is.

I might seem like I'm coming to AMD's defense like a good little fanboy would but I own a 4770k for a reason, the upgrade from Q6600 worked out lot bit better for the increased price was a no brainer but I wish it wasn't, we need AMD to shake things up again or 3~7% annual upgrades with premium prestige prices are all we will ever get.
